source: Mixed convection blowoff limits as a function of oxygen concentration and upward forced stretch rate for burning PMMA rods of various sizes (Marcum, Ferkul, Olson, ICES-2017-370)
quote: in good agreement with normal gravity buoyant flow velocities (~ 20 cm/s)
scope: Flames in normal gravity, cited to Hirano et al. 1974 in the paper
how_used: Centre of the 1 g buoyant flow range (15 to 25 cm/s).
caveat: Second-hand: the paper cites an older measurement. Not a rod-specific value.

source: Mixed convection blowoff limits as a function of oxygen concentration and upward forced stretch rate for burning PMMA rods of various sizes (Marcum, Ferkul, Olson, ICES-2017-370)
quote: an effective forced flow of 17 cm/s
quantity: Buoyant stretch expressed as forced flow, smallest rod (radius 0.318 cm)
how_used: Lower end of the 1 g buoyant flow range.
caveat: Found by shifting the 1 g blow-off data onto the BASS-II boundary, so it is not independent of the 16% figure in A3.

source: Combustion of Solids in Microgravity: Results from the BASS-II Experiment (poster, Ferkul et al., 2014)
quote: The 1g blowoff for the ¼" rod is at 16% oxygen
quantity: Oxygen at the 1 g blow-off limit
how_used: Fixes where the blow-off line crosses the 1 g buoyant flow, so the 1 g limit for rods is 16% by construction.
caveat: Applied to all four materials, which is an assumption. Precision of the 16% is not stated.

source: Mixed convection blowoff limits as a function of oxygen concentration and upward forced stretch rate for burning PMMA rods of various sizes (Marcum, Ferkul, Olson, ICES-2017-370)
quote: the normal gravity blowoff boundary for this axisymmetric rod geometry is determined to be linear, with oxygen concentration directly proportional to flow speed
scope: PMMA rods, five radii, 14 to 18% O2
how_used: Blow-off side is a straight line in oxygen against flow.
caveat: Rods only. The paper discards its 14% data as anomalous.

source: Microgravity flammability of PMMA rods in concurrent flow (Olson and Ferkul, 9th US National Combustion Meeting, 2015)

quantity: Zero-stretch intercept of the BASS-II blow-off line
how_used: Intercept of the blow-off line, sampled between 13.3 and 13.6%.

source: Mixed convection blowoff limits as a function of oxygen concentration and upward forced stretch rate for burning PMMA rods of various sizes (Marcum, Ferkul, Olson, ICES-2017-370)
quote: estimates that 13.4% O2 is the limiting oxygen concentration below which the fuel cannot burn at any stretch rate
quantity: Zero-stretch limit from the 1 g blow-off line
caveat: Rods only. Described by the authors as a conservative estimate.

source: Buoyancy Effects on Concurrent Flame Spread Over Thick PMMA
quote: the mixed convective flow velocity can be obtained by equating the boundary layer thickness for the mixed convective flow
quantity: Rule for combining forced flow and buoyant flow (Eq. 6: U_m = U_f (P/P0) [g^2 l_p^2 / U_f^4 + 1]^(1/4))
scope: Concurrent flame spread over thick PMMA, 1 g and reduced pressure
how_used: Central combination rule: U_eff = (U_f^4 + U_b^4)^(1/4). The sampled range runs from a linear sum to this rule.
caveat: The equation was read from the rendered page, not extracted as text. Derived for flame spread rate, not for flammability limits. The paper also scales by P/P0, which this model does not.

source: Mixed convection blowoff limits as a function of oxygen concentration and upward forced stretch rate for burning PMMA rods of various sizes (Marcum, Ferkul, Olson, ICES-2017-370)

quantity: Alternative rule for combining forced flow and buoyant flow
how_used: Lower end of the sampled combination exponent (linear sum).
caveat: Empirical, rods only, and the flows are aligned (upward forced flow with upward buoyancy).

source: Microgravity flammability of PMMA rods in concurrent flow (Olson and Ferkul, 9th US National Combustion Meeting, 2015)
quote: the quenching branch is captured with a red dashed exponential fit
how_used: Supports the exponential rise of the quench flow as oxygen falls, as in the model.

quote: In the normal gravity screening tests, flames extinguish by blowoff, where the buoyant flow is too fast
how_used: Supports reading the 1 g limit as a blow-off limit.

source: Combustion of Solids in Microgravity: Results from the BASS-II Experiment (poster, Ferkul et al., 2014)
quote: we obtained steady spreading at 13.6% oxygen in BASS-II
quantity: Lowest oxygen with steady spreading in microgravity
how_used: Model nose of the rod flammability boundary should sit near here.
caveat: Also appears in A5 and A6, which are used for the intercept. The quench side of the nose is not.

quote: reduced-g buoyancy or spacecraft ventilation flows of 5-20 cm/s
quantity: Flow level in reduced gravity (0 g, Lunar g, Martian g)
scope: Statement for reduced gravity in general
how_used: Model buoyant flow at 0.165 g and 0.38 g should fall inside this range.
caveat: Mixes buoyancy with ventilation, so it is a plausibility range only.

source: Combustion of Solids in Microgravity: Results from the BASS-II Experiment (poster, Ferkul et al., 2014)

quantity: Gap between the 1 g limit and the microgravity minimum
how_used: Model margin (1 g limit minus nose) compared with 1.4 to 2.4.
caveat: Equals 16% minus 13.6%, so it is partly the same data as A3 and H1.

quote: PMMA rods: Negative Oxygen Margin of Safety = 1.4% O2
quantity: Gap between the 1 g limit and the microgravity minimum
how_used: Second, lower margin figure from a later briefing.
caveat: The two margins differ and the sources do not say why.

source: Flammability Aspects of a Cotton-Fiberglass Fabric in Opposed and Concurrent Airflow in Microgravity (Ferkul, 2013)
quote: Downward flame spread (opposed flow) in 1-g with this material is not possible in normal air.
quantity: Outcome at 1 g, opposed flow, in air
scope: Cotton-fiberglass fabric (SIBAL), 21% O2, no forced flow
how_used: Model chance of burning for SIBAL, opposed, 1 g, 21% O2 should be below 50%.
caveat: A qualitative outcome. It is the only 1 g outcome found for opposed flow. The SAFFIRE-II ground tests (PSI-99) cover concurrent flow.
